item.title: Debugging a running .NET application with WinDbg and an AI agent
item.description: Every post in this series so far started from a file: a dump, a gcdump, a trace. That works as long as the answer is in memory at the moment the file is written. Some answers never are. A dump can show that a value is wrong. It cannot show who wrote it, because by the time the dump is taken, the write is long gone. That question needs a debugger attached to the running process, one that stops the process…

item.title: Database Performance: Counting Rows with EF Core vs. ADO.NET
item.description: Counting rows may seem simple, but the data-access approach can affect both execution time and memory allocations. This benchmark compares Entity Framework Core, compiled EF Core queries, and direct ADO.NET with SQLite to reveal which approach handles frequently executed count operations most efficiently. Worth a read for developers following .NET and Data. Link to article: https://dotnettips.com/2026/11/22/database-performance-counting-rows-with-ef-core-vs-ado-net

item.title: Finding a leak rooted by an event handler or a timer with an AI agent

This one has no cache, no static collection, and nothing that looks like storage. It leaks because objects subscribe to an event and because they schedule a timer. Same three commands, but the gcroot chain looks completely different, and the output is large enough that reading it becomes a problem of its…

item.title: Cut self-hosted LLM cost and latency with the distributed KV caching agent skill
item.description: Self-hosting LLMs on GPUs means paying to recompute the same context on every turn. Distributed KV caching with Amazon ElastiCache can cut inference cost by up to 40% and time to first token by up to 80%. This post walks through the distributed KV caching skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS, which evaluates and sets up the cache from your coding agent. Worth a read for developers following AI and AWS.

item.title: Diagnosing thread pool starvation from a .NET dump with an AI agent
item.description: Thread pool starvation does not hang the application, it makes it slow, and it makes it slow in a way that no profiler flags: the CPU is idle, no query is slow, and every individual operation looks fine. What is wrong is that the pool has no thread left to run the next work item, because the previous ones are all blocked waiting for something. This is also the case where an agent saves the most time,…
